claims.text: The stability of near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing at least five metals is governed primarily by the interplay of high mixing entropy and net negative enthalpy of mixing.
High mixing entropy and net negative enthalpy of mixing minimize the nanoparticles' free energy.
Free-energy minimization inhibits phase segregation and composition drift throughout 473–1923 K.
The initial material is a near-equiatomic, single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle containing at least five metallic elements.
Repeated thermal cycling from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic or thermoelectric environments provides the proposed stability test.
Mixing entropy and interatomic enthalpic interactions discourage phase segregation.
Mixing entropy and interatomic enthalpic interactions maintain a near-uniform elemental distribution.
High configurational entropy combined with favorable enthalpic interactions stabilizes a solid solution over a wide temperature range.
The proposed thermodynamic stabilization mitigates elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
After repeated operating-temperature exposure, the nanoparticles will largely retain a single-phase solid solution.
After thermal cycling, the nanoparticles will retain a nearly uniform elemental distribution.
Thermal cycling will cause only minimal changes in crystallography, local composition, and functional performance.
Comparable binary or ternary nanoparticles exhibit visible phase separation or compositional changes under similar conditions.
Critical nanoparticle size effects can enhance surface segregation.
Strong positive mixing enthalpy among selected components can overcome the stabilizing entropy contribution.
When size effects or strongly positive mixing enthalpy dominate, selective segregation or local structural transformations can occur.
Stability depends on the precise combination of metals, their enthalpic interactions, and the operating environment.
In situ XRD, EDS mapping, TEM, and functional measurements can test phase, compositional, microstructural, and performance stability.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly allows segregation when strongly positive mixing enthalpy overcomes entropy, but the experiment deliberately includes particles with varying mixing enthalpy and treats significant demixing or new phases as invalidating the hypothesis without excluding that stated boundary regime.

The boundary permits partial segregation or local structural transformations under size-driven conditions, whereas the falsification rule does not specify how much demixing or transformation is compatible with those exceptions.
